title: Three Prescriptions for Thinking More Clearly about Teaching, Part 2: Consume More Costly Things ume-more-costly-things/
author: Stuart Jr., Dave
summary: In the second part of his series on clear thinking, Dave Stuart Jr. argues that once teachers have cleared space by consuming fewer urgent things, they should fill it with costly ones. He defines costliness by what a work demanded from its maker and what it demands from the reader: a tweet, a blog post and a book of his own cost him very different amounts, and the book cost the reader the most time, thought and money. That higher cost is exactly what produces better thinking, because it forces sustained engagement, annotation, rereading and trying the strategies in the classroom. He adds caveats: costly can mean journal articles or a whole blog read deeply, not every book needs to be read cover to cover, and teachers should read widely beyond teaching, in areas like parenting, psychology and the history of science.
points: Costliness, measured in the reader's time, thought and money, is the criterion for what is worth reading if the goal is better thinking.
Real engagement with a book means annotating, discussing, rereading and testing its strategies in the classroom several times, which is why he favors reading fewer professional books.
Costly reading is not limited to books; research studies, long posts and a sustained read through one excellent blog can serve the same purpose.
Reading with a purpose, including skipping parts, and reading outside education are presented as wise rather than lazy.
quotes: And since flourishing teachers tend to do better work and enjoy their lives more than frustrated teachers do, this is no small matter. It's at the root of our mission to make teaching better.

The book. It cost me five years of my life. So, if you're going to read any of my things, and you want the fastest benefits to your thinking, I'd recommend the book first — here's the book — because it was costly.

While a tweet takes you a second to read and a blog post about five minutes, even an inspectional reading of a book will cost you an hour. If you find that a book has sufficient quality and value upon inspecting it, then a thorough analytical read of the book is likely to take a dozen hours.
Second, books demand more thought. You can get the gist of my tweet while being distracted; you can get the gist of my blog post pretty easily, too.
Costly things can be blogs. For a number of years I read Seth Godin's blog every day, plus a few of his books. The result is that I now have a good sense of how Seth thinks.
Not everything needs to be read the same. Your purpose drives the way you read. Most books that I read, I don't finish in the traditional sense of reading every single word.

Many of my best insights on teaching have come from books or articles on parenting, social psychology, Christian apologetics, and the history of science. When you've found a thread that's helping you answer one of your big, burning questions, here's the thing to do: keep pulling.
